To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) young children are able to make moral evaluations that consider the intentions underlying others’ actions, and (2) the extent to which they do so is influenced by the way that the task procedures highlight intention and outcome information.
young children’s moral evaluation is influenced by the relative saliencies of intention and outcome information.
the development of intention attribution and its integration into moral reasoning is influenced by the task procedures that present intention and outcome.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of moral evaluation in the preschool years, with a focus on the integration of intention and outcome information.
understanding the development of moral evaluation and how it is shaped by the social environment.
the development of intention attribution and its role in moral evaluation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the development of moral evaluation is a gradual and continuous process, in which children’s ability to consider intention and outcome information is enhanced with age and with the experience of social interaction.
intention attribution and its role in the development of moral evaluation is not a unitary process, but rather a multifaceted one.
young children’s moral evaluations are influenced by the relative predominance of intention or outcome information in task procedures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
young children’s moral evaluations are not solely based on outcomes, nor are they solely based on intentions.
young children’s moral evaluations are more likely to be driven by outcome than by intention when intention is not explicitly or directly available to them.
the development of moral evaluation involves a process of intention attribution and that intention attribution is influenced by the way that intention and outcome information is presented.
The main takeaway from our work is that
young children’s ability to generate intention-oriented moral judgments is highly sensitive to task procedures.
the development of moral evaluation may not be a simple, linear process but instead a more nuanced one that is influenced by the way that intention and outcome are presented.
intention attribution is not a unitary process but rather a multifaceted one that is shaped by the specific task procedures used to elicit it.
